newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's "dream" election hopes fading away.
newsitem.headline: Japan's "dream" election hopes fading away.

text.p: A general election meant to catapult Japan into the 21st century is turning into a sad "don't know, don't care" poll, far from the dreamy hopes that it could restore faith in Japan Inc.
Seldom can an election loftily described as a "landmark" and "turning point" have caused so much pessimism before the result is even known.

Warnings by political leaders, from Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto to main opposition leader Ichiro Ozawa, that the October 20 election is the last chance to revitalise Japan before it falls into decline, have fallen on deaf ears.
"This election will determine whether the dream of a revitalised Japan can be realised," Hashimoto told rallies in the opening days of the campaign this week.
"This election will clarify whether Japanese society will be reborn through reform or fall into decline through the continuation of do-nothing policies," Ozawa said.
But their dire warnings do not appear to be have stirred the nation's 98 million potential voters.
Polls forecast a record low turnout. More than half the electorate say they have no idea whom to support and the same number say they are confused by a complex new electoral system.
One poll found that 43 percent of the electorate did not know in which constituency they belonged.
Many of the commentaries and editorials have been equally bleak in assessing that come the counting there will be no winners, just politics as usual.

"We may go so far as to say that all parties, with the exception of the Communists, are drifting with no real purpose and are merely going through the motions," the Mainichi Shimbun said last Tuesday on the opening day of official campaigning.

Rather than a leadership mandate for either Hashimoto or Ozawa, bets on who will rule range from a "Government of National Salvation" involving both men to a result decided by the fledgling Democratic Party of recent defectors from the LDP-led coalition government.
It was not meant to be like this three years ago when the last election was held in a giddy mood of political change.
In the interim there have been four prime ministers, including Hashimoto for the last nine months.
The turmoil of constant party realignments might have been worth the trouble if out of the revolving door strides a newly decisive two-party Japan.

Instead, the choice is essentially the same as it has been since the end of World War Two -- who can capture or topple Hashimoto's long-ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) or wound it enough to join the LDP as a junior coalition partner.
Former LDP men even riddle the opposition from Ozawa, head of Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) to Yukio Hatoyama, co-leader of the three-week-old Democratic Party.

The pro-business, pro-Washington LDP has long been regarded as the only party that could get things done in Japan. But it was also called the "necessary evil" because of corrupt, behind-the-scenes methods which came to roost when the LDP lost power for the first time in 38 years in the 1993 election.
The LDP was only in the wilderness for a year before regaining government in mid-1994 in an unholy coalition with the leftist Socialists and Sakigake, an LDP splinter group.

Last January Hashimoto, 59, a tough former trade minister and traditional Japanese sword fighter, captured the prime minister's job for the party when Socialist leader Tomiichi Murayama stepped down from the post he held for 18 months, setting the scene for this month's election.

Under the present 511-seat parliament, the LDP has 211 seats, Shinshinto 160, the Democrats 52, the Socialists 30, the Communists 15, Sakigake nine, minor parties six, independents 10 and 18 seats are vacant.

In the new electoral system, there are 300 single seat constituencies and 200 decided by proportional representation in 11 regional blocs. The system does away with multi-seat constituencies to end pork-barrel electioneering and put the emphasis on party politics.
The main players, the LDP and Shinshinto, are essentially conservative parties with tax levels the only substantive difference to emerge in their campaign promises so far.
The LDP wants to raise the national sales tax from three to five percent while Shinshinto wants to delay the rise for several years and stimulate the economy with income tax cuts.
Both parties favour cutting back the power of civil servants, the country's favourite villains at present because of a series of scandals.
No one knows exactly where the drive and high hopes for dramatic political change went wrong.

Was there just too much party turmoil in the past three years? Did 1995's devastating Kobe earthquake and subway poison gas attacks end dreams? Did the bursting of Japan's economic "bubble" leave room only for making a livelihood in the present, not building a 21st century Japan?

"To the extent that can be measured in polls, voters do not have much interest in the election, even though they have a chance to shape the political future," the Asahi Shimbun lamented in an assessment of the electorate's mood.
